current_public_record.title: Detection of AI-Generated Synthetic Images with a Lightweight CNN
current_public_record.abstract: The rapid development of generative adversarial networks has significantly advanced the generation of synthetic images, presenting valuable opportunities and ethical dilemmas in their potential misuse across various industries. The necessity to distinguish real from AI-generated content is becoming increasingly critical to preserve the integrity of online data. While traditional methods for detecting fake images resulting from image tampering rely on hand-crafted features, the sophistication of manipulated images produced by generative adversarial networks requires more advanced detection approaches. The lightweight approach proposed here is based on convolutional neural networks that comprise only eight convolutional and two hidden layers that effectively differentiate AI-generated images from real ones. The proposed approach was assessed using two benchmark datasets and custom-generated data from Sentinel-2 imagery. It demonstrated superior performance compared to four state-of-the-art methods on the CIFAKE dataset, achieving the highest accuracy of 97.32%, on par with the highest-performing state-of-the-art method. Explainable AI is utilized to enhance our comprehension of the complex processes involved in synthetic image recognition. We have shown that, unlike authentic images, where activations often center around the main object, in synthetic images, activations cluster around the edges of objects, in the background, or in areas with complex textures.

current_public_record.title: A Survey of Detection and Mitigation for Fake Images on Social Media Platforms
current_public_record.abstract: Recently, the spread of fake images on social media platforms has become a significant concern for individuals, organizations, and governments. These images are often created using sophisticated techniques to spread misinformation, influence public opinion, and threaten national security. This paper begins by defining fake images and their potential impact on society, including the spread of misinformation and the erosion of trust in digital media. This paper also examines the different types of fake images and their challenges for detection. We then review the recent approaches proposed for detecting fake images, including digital forensics, machine learning, and deep learning. These approaches are evaluated in terms of their strengths and limitations, highlighting the need for further research. This paper also highlights the need for multimodal approaches that combine multiple sources of information, such as text, images, and videos. Furthermore, we present an overview of existing datasets, evaluation metrics, and benchmarking tools for fake image detection. This paper concludes by discussing future directions for fake image detection research, such as developing more robust and explainable methods, cross-modal fake detection, and the integration of social context. It also emphasizes the need for interdisciplinary research that combines computer science, digital forensics, and cognitive psychology experts to tackle the complex problem of fake images. This survey paper will be a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working on fake image detection on social media platforms.

original_contributions.description: A taxonomy and narrative synthesis of forensic/semantic/statistical/web-retrieval/neural/multimodal fake-image detection, literature performance comparisons, existing resource and metric catalog, and research challenges.

question_matrix.question: Is the primary contribution a survey of existing methods?
question_matrix.finding: Yes. Section 1.3 lists comprehensive coverage, summarized performance comparisons, emphasis on deep learning, future challenges and information on existing datasets/metrics. Figure 5 supplies a detection taxonomy, Figure 6 explains generic detection workflows, Sections 4–5 synthesize cited methods, and the conclusion reiterates survey findings. The paper has 138 numbered references, not an independently specified new detector or benchmark section.

question_matrix.question: Are technical comparisons literature-sourced or independently re-executed?
question_matrix.finding: Tables 1–7 attribute rows to named source works and reference numbers. Page 25 expressly says att-RNN results are taken from Khattar and that the original att-RNN literature is not discussed. The text describes each cited method and its reported evaluation, without supplying a common re-execution environment, model checkpoints, splits, training schedules or survey-specific run outputs. This supports literature-derived comparisons. The first-person Fakeddit experiment statement on p.27 is genuine unresolved counterevidence; it prevents asserting that the authors never performed any experiment. It does not identify a reproducible survey-specific benchmark.

question_matrix.question: Does the paper contribute an original experimental benchmark?
question_matrix.finding: No separately substantive original experimental benchmark is established by the complete manuscript. The tabulated outputs are attributed source-method results on existing datasets. There is no identified new benchmark name, original survey evaluation dataset, method-independent experimental output or new test-set construction tied to those tables. This is a finding about the published contribution, not proof that no unpublished or unreported experiments occurred.

question_matrix.question: Is a new evaluation protocol explicitly defined?
question_matrix.finding: The paper states a comparison-selection rule: techniques are compared when metric and dataset match (§4 p.8); it repeats accuracy/similar-dataset selection for Table 5 and similar-parameter/dataset selection for Table 6. This is positive comparative-framework evidence. However, these general grouping criteria and Figure 6 generic workflows do not specify a new operational evaluation protocol, common sample IDs, split/threshold rules, baseline retraining procedure, or a new scoring construction that can be applied as this paper's distinct contribution. No mandatory code requirement is imposed.
question_matrix.locator: §4 p.8; Figure 6 p.6; Table 5 introduction p.16; Table 6 discussion p.21

question_matrix.question: Is a new reusable challenge or test resource provided?
question_matrix.finding: No separately contributed challenge or test resource is identified. Section 6.2 catalogs known external datasets. Section 7.1 calls for new continuously updated labeled datasets and Section 7.2 calls for cross-platform/multi-source training as future work. These motivations are useful research challenges, but the paper does not instantiate a new standardized challenge/test collection for others.

question_matrix.question: Are dataset descriptions summaries of existing resources?
question_matrix.finding: Yes. Table 10 contains 14 catalog rows with historical source collections, access dates and external hosts: BuzzFeed, CASIA1.0, CASIA2.0, CelebA, a row called COCO whose description refers to INRIA Holidays/Copydays, Columbia, CoMoFoD, FakeNewsNet, FNC, MediaEval2015, NIST Nimble16, PGGAN, PHEME and Weibo. Fakeddit is additionally discussed in the text and attributed as an existing benchmark in reference 127. Entries marked self-made describe source datasets, not an established new dataset produced by this survey. Resource identity/count inconsistencies remain as printed and were not externally resolved.
question_matrix.locator: §6.2 pp.26–28; Table 10 p.28; reference 127 p.36

question_matrix.question: Are metrics newly proposed or existing measures reviewed?
question_matrix.finding: Existing measures are reviewed. Table 8 gives a conventional binary confusion matrix and Table 9 lists precision, recall, accuracy, F1, false-positive rate, false-negative rate, HTER, ROC, AUROC and a row spelled mPA that describes mean average precision. The paper presents these as prominent measures already used by researchers. FPR/FNR/HTER denominator parentheses are ambiguous as printed; they are not silently corrected or treated as new metric definitions.
question_matrix.locator: §6.1 and Table 8 p.26; Table 9 p.27

question_matrix.question: Do comparative tables establish an independently original benchmark framework?
question_matrix.finding: They establish a structured comparative survey organized by detection category, dataset and metric, with pros/cons and representative performance. A permissive R2 reading could value this as a reusable systematic comparative framework. Under the established conservative separate-contribution threshold, the evidence remains a synthesis/catalog of published evaluations, without a separately specified method-evaluation procedure, challenge or benchmark resource beyond that synthesis. The proposed removal does not follow merely from the paper being a survey or from a lack of newly generated images.

question_matrix.question: Is an original benchmark implementation, standardized split or protocol released?
question_matrix.finding: No original benchmark implementation, immutable sample/split list, evaluation package or distinct protocol release is established in the paper. The Data Availability Statement points to publicly available datasets and links in references. Table 10 links external resource providers. No linked assets, code archives or supplements were downloaded; actual current availability of each dataset was not tested. Absence of code alone is not the reason to remove benchmark.
question_matrix.locator: Table 10 p.28; Data Availability Statement p.31

question_matrix.question: Is the central contribution taxonomy, synthesis and research challenges?
question_matrix.finding: Yes. Figure 5 organizes image-based fake-news detection, Sections 3–5 survey tampering techniques and methods, and Section 7 synthesizes eight challenge areas: labeled datasets, cross-platform training, satire versus fake, interpretability, audio splicing, multimodal detection, deepfakes and active methods. The conclusion calls for further multimodal research and larger real-time labeled datasets. Survey is strongly supported and no survey removal is proposed.

question_matrix.question: Is any independent benchmark contribution substantiated?
question_matrix.finding: The strongest possible evidence is the stated performance-comparison contribution, the same-metric/dataset grouping principle and the isolated first-person Fakeddit two-way-label experiment description. These are preserved rather than dismissed. But no Fakeddit result column, named survey model, split specification, scoring procedure or run is connected to that clause in Tables 5–7 or the rest of the manuscript. Selecting an existing binary label convention does not by itself establish a new reusable benchmark contribution, even if some experiment was performed. Its intended referent remains unresolved without further evidence.
question_matrix.locator: §1.3 p.4; §4 p.8; Tables 5–7 pp.16,24,26; Fakeddit bullet §6.2 p.27

question_matrix.question: Is retaining both survey and benchmark scientifically defensible?
question_matrix.finding: The permissive interpretation is defensible as a policy reading: an openly available, organized comparison and source catalog can be reused for method selection, and R2 allows systematic comparative frameworks without new code/data. The competing conservative reading distinguishes a useful comparative survey from a separately substantive evaluation contribution. On the full published evidence, benchmark removal is provisionally supported under that conservative threshold, yielding survey only. The policy judgment has medium confidence; the survey identity and literature attribution are high-confidence findings. Maintainer acceptance remains pending.
